verses.1: Al-Mizan reads al-Raḥmān as a hyperbolic name denoting abundant raḥma expressed through generous blessings. It encompasses the blessings received by believers and disbelievers in this world and those exclusive to believers in the hereafter, so its universality suits a chapter concerning benefits that order the lives of humankind and jinn in both worlds. Unlike names such as al-Raḥīm and al-Rāḥim, it is exclusive to God. Teaching the Qur’an heads the enumeration because it is God’s direct speech, the greatest blessing, guiding to felicity and revealed for the education of humans and jinn. Although the recipient is unstated, the commentary judges the joint reading more likely because the chapter addresses both in the dual; readings that make the recipient Muḥammad or Gabriel are less appropriate.

verses.3: Al-Mizan takes ‘man’ to mean the human species, God’s most wondrous creation, for whom the path to perfection is laid out outwardly and inwardly, in this world and the next; yet humans may fall except through faith and righteous deeds (95:4–6). Bayān, literally uncovering, is the power to disclose what is in the mind. By innate divine inspiration, humans turn vocal sounds into letters and signs for absent sensible things and for intelligible ideas, presenting them to another mind as if present. This capacity makes civil society, mutual understanding, and human progress possible. The diversity of languages, shaped by peoples’ dispositions and regions, is evidence of this innate guidance (30:22). God did not create particular languages and reveal them ready-made; He endowed humans with a fiṭra inclined to society, through which they conventionally associate words with meanings and devise writing to represent speech. This gift preserves human life and guides it toward every good. Interpretations identifying man with Adam or Muḥammad, or bayān with names, the Qur’an, good and evil, or guidance and error, are judged far from the apparent meaning.

verses.5: Al-Mizan explains ḥusbān as a verbal noun meaning accounting: the sun and moon run according to God’s calculation. Najm may denote trunkless plants, an interpretation supported by its pairing with ‘tree,’ although the preceding mention of the sun and moon makes ‘star’ possible. Their prostration is not merely obedience to a command: plants extend roots and veins beneath the earth for water and minerals, manifesting their innate need for the God who sustains them. The commentary notes that the grammar makes both verses predicates of the All-beneficent. It reports al-Kashshāf’s view that their obvious semantic connection removes any need for an explicit one, and that the earlier unconnected enumeration rebukes those who deny God’s bounties before the discourse returns to its usual connective form.

verses.7: Al-Mizan takes ‘raised’ in its physical sense if the sky is the upward direction, created high, or the celestial bodies appointed above the earth after their separation (21:30). If it is the place of the angels’ stations and the source of divine command and revelation, the raising is spiritual or combines spiritual and physical senses. It finds the broader reading of mīzān as justice, by which each receives their due, more comprehensive than the reading of it as a weighing instrument.
verses.8: Al-Mizan takes mīzān here primarily as the ordinary weighing scale: God’s setting it up requires just weights and forbids depriving others of their due. If the preceding mīzān is the more general standard of rights or justice, this is a particular practical rule derived from that principle. It reads allā taṭghaw as explanatory, formed from an and lā, with lā taṭghaw a prohibition; qisṭ means the same as ʿadl. The prohibition on shortening the balance explains and intensifies infringement by barring a loss to either buyer or seller. The alternative reading that makes the balance accusative and the phrase a negation would require an awkward connection between an imperative and a declarative sentence.

verses.10: Al-Mizan notes that anām may mean humankind, humankind and jinn, or every creature that crawls on land. It also contrasts the earth being ‘laid out’ (waḍʿ) with the sky being ‘raised’ (rafʿ).
verses.11: Al-Mizan defines fākiha as every kind of fruit other than dates and akmām as the coverings of date bunches. It reports that kumm in the sense of a garment is never spelt kimm.
verses.12: Al-Mizan reads the verse as joined to the preceding list: ḥabb is the edible part of crops such as grain, barley, and rice, while ʿaṣf is their outer husk. It notes readings of ʿaṣf as crop leaves or dried crop leaves, and glosses rayḥān as fragrant herbs.
verses.13: Al-Mizan defines alāʾ as the plural of ilan, ‘blessing,’ and takes the dual address to be jointly to humankind and jinn, as the direct addresses in (55:31), (55:33), and (55:35) show. It rejects readings that make it male and female humankind or an emphatic dual addressed to one individual. The chapter counts even resurrection, punishment, and the requital of wrongdoers among divine blessings because assigning each being its fitting consequence sustains the universal order, just as coercion against the corrupt serves an entire human society. Hell’s punishment and paradise’s reward are therefore blessings in relation to all human and jinn-kind, as are the chapter’s cosmic benefits. This also shows that jinn share in the enumerated blessings.
verses.14: Al-Mizan defines ṣalṣāl as clay dried and hardened until it makes a clinking sound when trodden. It takes insān as the human species, whose created form will become such clay, while noting the alternative of Adam. Mārij is a pure spark of fire, though some call it fire mixed with soot; as clay is the human species’ eventual created form, fire is that of the jinn species. The alternative reading identifies the jinn with their first progenitor.

verses.16: Al-Mizan refers this repeated question to its explanation at verse 13.
verses.17: Al-Mizan ordinarily takes the two easts as the winter and summer points of sunrise, whose change orders the seasons and creatures’ sustenance. It notes another reading in which they are the sun’s and moon’s rising points, with the two wests their setting points.
verses.18: Al-Mizan refers this repeated question to its explanation at verse 13.
verses.19: Al-Mizan reads maraja as mixing rather than sending, and the two seas as fresh and salt water, as in (35:12). It rejects a reference to two particular seas in favour of two kinds: the salt oceans and seas, and fresh water held in underground reservoirs, emerging in springs and flowing through rivers. They continuously meet, yet physical reservoirs and a nonphysical safeguard prevent salt water from directly contaminating fresh water and prevent fresh water from overwhelming the seas and removing the benefits of their saltiness. Rain carried from the seas replenishes fresh sources, while rivers replenish the seas. Thus neither can overwhelm the other and destroy the natural order that sustains life.

verses.22: Al-Mizan says pearls and coral emerge from both the fresh and salt seas, one benefit their combined existence supplies to humankind.
verses.23: Al-Mizan refers this repeated question to its explanation at verse 13.
verses.24: Al-Mizan glosses jawārī as ships, munshaʾāt as brought forth and nurtured, and aʿlām as mountains. Although ships are made by humans, they belong to God because their materials and the maker’s senses, intellect, and will are created by Him, as are whatever these creations produce. Human knowledge of manufacture, its benefits, and their use is itself a divine blessing.
verses.25: Al-Mizan refers this repeated question to its explanation at verse 13.
verses.26: Al-Mizan understands everyone on earth to mean every sentient and thinking being, including humankind and jinn, who will perish when this worldly creation ends and a new creation of recompense begins. This is not total annihilation but return to God, and is a blessing because worldly life is the preliminary step toward the hereafter. God’s Face is His noble names and attributes, such as knowledge, power, mercy, forgiveness, and provision, through which He relates to creation and sends blessing and guidance. Jalāl denotes the attributes of elevation, authority, and overpowering, while ikrām denotes the splendor and attraction associated with attributes such as knowledge, life, mercy, generosity, and beauty; these are respectively the attributes of majesty (ṣifāt al-jalāl) and beauty (ṣifāt al-jamāl). Dhū al-jalāl wa al-ikrām unites both kinds of names and ultimately refers to the divine essence. The focus on Face may mean that the phrase praises the Lord rather than qualifies Face, or that Face itself is the divine name of munificence. If Face is a divine name, its subsistence depends on God, who remains unchanged by creation’s passing. If it is the means by which God turns to creation, it includes what is attributed to or near Him—such as prophets, representatives, religion, reward, and nearness—which survives, as (16:96) says.

verses.29: Al-Mizan takes every being’s asking as its innate neediness and utter contingency upon God, in the sense found in (35:15) and (14:34). The indefiniteness of shaʾn stresses the diverse work through which, at every moment, God acts in a way unlike what preceded or follows; He never repeats an action or performs one resembling another, but originates without precedent, ibdāʿ (2:117). ‘Every day’ therefore signifies an all-encompassing agency: He is present at every time and place and with everything, yet is contained by neither time nor place and does not approach anything.
verses.30: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.31: Al-Mizan explains farāgh, making oneself unoccupied for a matter, as setting aside prior concerns to devote full attention to something important. God’s declaration therefore means that the original creation will be brought to its close and attention turned to jinn and humankind in their resurrection, judgment, and recompense, through a transformation into a new creation. This does not conflict with lā yashghaluhu shaʾnun ʿan shaʾnin, for the verse concerns the succession of creations, whereas that principle concerns God’s omnipotence and omnipresence; likewise, (55:29) concerns the variety of His works. Al-thaqalān denotes jinn and humankind, and the plural pronouns are used because those two grammatical groups contain multitudes of individuals.
verses.32: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.33: Al-Mizan takes this as a Day of Resurrection challenge to jinn and humankind, exposing their incapacity to flee God’s dominion and punishment; jinn are mentioned first because they move faster than humans. Istiṭāʿa means qudra, aqṭār are regions or quarters, and passing through means escaping across the confines of heaven and earth. Sulṭān principally means existential power (qudra wujūdiyya), though it can also mean conclusive proof or sovereignty; they have none. The reading that the verse concerns penetrating heaven and earth through knowledge is judged incompatible with its context.
verses.34: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.35: Al-Mizan reports Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī’s definition of shuwāẓ as a flame without smoke and Majmaʿ al-Bayān’s similar description of a green flame separated from fire. It notes that nuḥās is also glossed by al-Rāghib as a flame without smoke. The inability to help one another means that none can aid another against the tribulation or escape it, because the system of causes and effects in the hereafter differs from this world and affords no protection from God.
verses.36: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.37: Al-Mizan says the sky will split open and turn crimson like tanned leather.
verses.38: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.39: Al-Mizan places this verse within the Day of Resurrection’s judgment and recompense, describing the transgressors, those who fear their Lord’s station, and both groups’ outcomes. The absence of questioning denotes the swiftness of judgment, as in (24:39), but does not conflict with verses that say people will be questioned, including (37:24) and (15:92). The Day has different stages: people may be questioned in some, mouths may be sealed and limbs made to speak in others, and some may be known by their mark.
verses.40: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.41: Al-Mizan reads the verse as the implicit answer to why the guilty are not questioned: visible marks on their faces identify them, after which they are seized by forelocks and feet and thrown into hellfire. Its fresh, unconnected construction suits that answer. Nawāṣī means the hair at the front of the head, and aqdām means feet; ‘by the forelocks’ grammatically occupies the position of the doer of the passive verb ‘seized.’
verses.42: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.43: Al-Mizan takes these words as what the guilty will be told on the Day of Resurrection: this is the hell they denied, through which they will move between its fire and extreme boiling water. It reports al-Ṭabrisī’s possible reading that the words are addressed to the Prophet about the guilty among his people. Ḥamīm means hot water and ānin denotes its extreme heat.

verses.46: Al-Mizan understands God’s standing, maqām, first as His standing over servants’ deeds: His comprehensive knowledge, preservation, and recompense of them, as in (13:33). It may instead be a noun of place denoting His lordly position in managing their affairs, sending messengers to call to faith and good works, decreeing recompense, and encompassing what they say and do. The fear here is not fear of punishment for disobedience or desire for reward—the worship of the slave and the merchant—but humility and submission before God’s greatness. Those who fear in this sense worship sincerely for His countenance alone, as angels do in (16:50); the commentary identifies them with the devoted, ahl al-ikhlāṣ, and considers it not unlikely that they are the Foremost Ones, sābiqūn, brought near in (56:7–11). The suggested explanations for why there are two gardens—separate homes, rewards for belief and deeds, rewards for deeds and avoiding sin, or corporeal and spiritual gardens—are all said to lack evidence. One possible reading, however, is that one garden is recompense (thawāb) and the other grace (faḍl), deduced from (50:35).
verses.47: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.48: Al-Mizan preserves two readings of afnān: as the plural of fann, it means varieties and describes gardens with diverse fruits and the like; as the plural of fanan, it means supple branches and describes trees full of them.
verses.49: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.50: Al-Mizan says the indefinite description of the two flowing springs magnifies their importance.
verses.51: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.52: Al-Mizan takes the phrase to mean two types of every fruit and judges the proposal of a known worldly type and an unseen type, along with other interpretations, unsupported by evidence.
verses.53: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.54: Al-Mizan glosses furush as beds, baṭāʾin as their interior rather than exterior, and istabraq as thick silk. It reports Majmaʿ al-Bayān’s inference that brocade on the interior implies an even more luxurious exterior. Janā means harvested fruit, and dānin, from danuww, means close at hand; the gardens’ harvested fruit is therefore nearby.
verses.55: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.56: Al-Mizan says the feminine plural hinna may refer to the beds or to the gardens, since each of God’s friends has two. Ṭarf literally means eyelid, and restrained glances signify satisfaction with their spouses and no desire for another. Their being untouched by human or jinn means they were never married or had intercourse before their spouses in paradise.
verses.57: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.58: Al-Mizan takes rubies and corals as an image of purity of colour, splendor, and brightness.
verses.59: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.60: Al-Mizan reads the rhetorical question as explaining why the inhabitants of paradise receive two gardens: their goodness, performed in fear of their Lord’s standing, is recompensed with goodness. The verse establishes paradise and its blessings as recompense for deeds. It does not itself address the excess grace, faḍl, indicated elsewhere, unless iḥsān is held incomplete unless it exceeds the doer’s goodness; then the word goodness would include that excess.
verses.61: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.62: Al-Mizan takes min dūnihimā, beneath the first two gardens, as lower in rank, divine grace, and nobility, even if similar in blessings. The first pair belongs to those devoted and sincere believers who fear their Lord’s standing, while the lower pair belongs to believers of lesser rank, including those who worship from fear of hell or desire for paradise: the Companions of the Right, aṣḥāb al-yamīn. It records the alternative that min dūnihimā means close to them, making these gardens the first owners’ gardens, and the claim that they are superior; but the division between the Brought Near, al-muqarrabūn, and the Companions of the Right supports its own reading.
verses.63: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.64: Al-Mizan says the colour is a deep green approaching black, reflecting the trees’ verdancy.
verses.65: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.66: Al-Mizan reads the springs as gushing forcefully from their source.
verses.67: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.68: Al-Mizan says ‘fruits’ and ‘pomegranates’ here mean fruit trees and pomegranate trees, as nakhl, ‘date palm’ rather than ‘date,’ indicates.
verses.69: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.70: Al-Mizan says the plural hinna may treat these two gardens as one pair among many; other readings make it refer to all four gardens or to the fruit, date palms, and pomegranate trees. Khayr commonly concerns abstract qualities and ḥasan tangible forms, so khayrāt ḥisān means the maidens are beautiful in character and appearance.
verses.71: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.72: Al-Mizan says khiyām is the plural of khayma, a tent or encampment. The houris’ seclusion, maqṣūrāt, signifies chastity rather than licentiousness: none has access to them except their partners.
verses.73: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.74: Al-Mizan refers this to the earlier explanation of their untouched state.
verses.75: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.76: Al-Mizan cites al-Ṣiḥāḥ’s definition of rafraf as green fabric used for seating, while reporting readings of it as pillows and other meanings. Khuḍr is the plural of akhḍar and qualifies rafraf. It reports that ʿabqarī may mean a carpet, pile rug, woven fabric, or brocade.
verses.77: The same question is explained at verse 13.
verses.78: Al-Mizan says the verse praises God for blessings throughout this world and the hereafter that descend through His all-encompassing mercy. The Name is al-Raḥmān, the All-beneficent with which the chapter began, and tabāruk means abounding and overflowing in good and blessing: God so named is blessed for His abundant gifts. ‘Lord of majesty and honour’ points to the Beautiful Names arising from divine attributes, whose effects appear in and cause His acts. He creates and orders through being badīʿ, khāliq, and mubdiʾ, does so proficiently through being ʿalīm and ḥakīm, rewards the obedient through being wadūd, shakūr, ghafūr, and raḥīm, and punishes sinners through being muntaqim and shadīd al-ʿiqāb. The title thus highlights the Beautiful Names, asmāʾ al-ḥusnāʾ, and lofty attributes, ṣifāt al-ʿulyāʾ, from which blessings and gifts emanate.
